articles.title: Podcast an issue, fairly

body.support:
You know how to make a podcast. An **issue** podcast has three more jobs: show both sides, use evidence, and credit it all.

**1. Pick an issue.** Choose something people argue about. Something you care about.

**2. Research both sides.** Find two good sources for each side. Write down where you found them.

**3. Plan your parts.**

- **Start:** a voice or question to grab them.
- **Intro:** what's the issue?
- **Side A,** with evidence.
- **Side B,** with evidence.
- **What I think,** and why.
- **End:** say where your sources are.

**4. Real voices.** Ask people short questions. Always ask if you can record them first.

**5. Your view.** Say: *“I think ___, because ___.”*

**6. Credit it.** Say your sources out loud. List them in your show notes.

**7. Check it.** Did both sides get a fair go? Are the facts right?
body.core:
You already know how to make a podcast: plan it, script it, record it, edit it. An **issue episode** adds three big jobs: show more than one side, back everything with evidence, and credit it all.

**1. Pick a real issue.** Choose something people genuinely disagree about, and that you care about. Local and close-to-home issues work best: transport, jobs, sport, school, your town.

**2. Research both sides.** Find at least two **reliable** sources for each main **perspective**. Look for the *strongest* version of the side you disagree with, not the weakest. Write down every reference as you go: who, title, date and link.

**3. Plan a run sheet.** A **run sheet** maps your episode, segment by segment:

- **Cold open:** a voice, a sound or a question that grabs attention.
- **Intro:** the show, the issue, and why it matters.
- **Side A:** the main argument, with evidence and a voice.
- **Side B:** the other argument, given a fair go.
- **Where I land:** your point of view, with your best evidence.
- **Outro:** a call to action, and where to find the sources.

**4. Get real voices.** Short **vox pops** (quick interviews) bring an issue to life. Always ask for **consent**, explain how you'll use the recording, and quote people accurately. Don't record anyone who says no.

**5. Argue your view.** Being fair doesn't mean having no opinion. After both sides, say where you land, and why: *“I think ___, because ___. The strongest evidence is ___.”*

**6. Credit everything.** Say key sources aloud: *“According to…”*. Put full references and music credits in your **show notes**. Use only music you're allowed to use.

**7. Edit and check.** Cut mistakes and long pauses. Then check: did each side get a fair go? Are the facts right? Is everything credited?

**8. Share it safely.** Share with your class or school, or on a platform your teacher approves. Check everyone in it is happy to be heard.
body.extend:
You already know the production cycle: plan, script, record, edit. An **issue episode** adds three demands: represent multiple perspectives fairly, support claims with evidence, and attribute everything.

**1. Choose a contested issue.** Pick something people genuinely disagree about, and that you care about. Local issues (transport, work, sport, school, your town) tend to make the strongest episodes.

**2. Research the perspectives.** Find at least two **reliable** sources for each main **perspective**. Seek the *strongest* version of the view you oppose. Record full references as you go.

**3. Build a run sheet.** A **run sheet** maps the episode:

- **Cold open:** a voice, sound or question that hooks.
- **Intro:** show, issue and stakes.
- **Perspective A:** argument, evidence and a voice.
- **Perspective B:** the same treatment, fairly.
- **Where I land:** your position, justified.
- **Outro:** call to action and where to find sources.

**4. Gather voices ethically.** **Vox pops** add authenticity. Obtain **consent**, explain how recordings will be used, and quote accurately.

**5. Argue your position.** A **balanced** episode can still end with a clear view. Justify it with your strongest evidence, and acknowledge what the other side gets right.

**6. Attribute everything.** Name key sources aloud and give full references and music credits in the **show notes**. Use only licensed or original music.

**7. Edit and verify.** Tighten the audio. Then audit it: is each perspective fairly represented, is every fact accurate, and is every source credited?

**8. Publish responsibly.** Share through approved channels, and confirm everyone featured is comfortable being heard.

caseStudies.title: The Daily Aus

body.support:
In **2017**, two young Australians started **The Daily Aus**. They wanted to explain the news to young people in plain words. They started on **Instagram**.

The Daily Aus says it doesn't take sides in politics. It explains what's happening. It shows the different views. Then readers decide.

Later, it started a **daily news podcast**.

More young people now get news on social media. The Daily Aus shows news can be clear, fair and not boring.

Your podcast can do the same. But at the end, you'll say what *you* think.
body.core:
In **2017**, two young Australians, **Sam Koslowski** and **Zara Seidler**, started **The Daily Aus**. Their idea was simple. Explain the news to young people, in plain words, in the places young people already were. They started on **Instagram**.

The Daily Aus says it is **independent** and **non-partisan**. That means it doesn't back a political party. It aims to explain what's going on and why it matters. It sets out the different views on an issue, so readers can make up their own minds.

Later, it started a **daily news podcast**. Each weekday morning, the team covers the news in an everyday voice.

This matters because of where young people get their news. In 2025, a University of Canberra report found that more Australians now name **social media** as their main news source than news websites. That was a first.

The Daily Aus shows an issue can be explained clearly and fairly, in a young voice, without being boring. It doesn't tell people what to think. That's a good model for your episode, with one change. At the end of yours, you'll say where *you* land.
body.extend:
In **2017**, **Sam Koslowski** and **Zara Seidler** started **The Daily Aus**. Their aim was to explain the news to young Australians in plain language, on the apps they already used. It began on **Instagram**.

The Daily Aus describes itself as **independent** and **non-partisan**. It doesn't side with a political party. It aims to explain issues and set out the main views, so its audience can decide for themselves.

Later, it launched a **daily news podcast**: a weekday-morning briefing in a relaxed, everyday voice.

This fits a bigger shift. In 2025, the University of Canberra's Digital News Report found that **social media** had overtaken news websites as a main source of news. It was the first time that had happened.

The Daily Aus shows that an issue can be explained clearly and fairly, in a voice that suits young people. Your episode borrows that approach, with one addition. After you present the different views, you'll argue your own.

teacher.answers:
**Check your reading:** show more than one side, back everything with evidence, credit it all. Cold open, intro, side A, side B, where I land, outro. Ask for consent and explain how you'll use the recording.

**Run sheet:** 1 cold open (vox pop hook, consent noted); 2 intro; 3 side A with a credited source; 4 side B, a fair go; 5 where I land, with evidence; 6 outro with call to action and credits.

**Case study:** The Daily Aus explains issues and sets out perspectives so audiences decide; an opinion podcast argues one view. Instagram is where its young audience already was. Your episode explains both sides, then adds your own justified view.

realityCheck: **Topic choice makes or breaks it.** Local, concrete issues beat big abstract ones.
**Vox pops take time and nerve.** Let students interview family, staff or classmates if public recording isn't practical.
**Fairness is hard when you care.** The fairness check with a listener is the key moment; build in time for it.
**Keep sharing safe.** Default to class or school audiences unless everyone has consented to wider sharing.
**Works in a real class:** yes. It's a portfolio piece students can show employers or TAFE.
